'''Valery Leonidovich Pokrovsky''' ({{langx|ru|Валерий Леонидович Покровский}}; born 1 January 1931) is a [[USSR|Soviet]] and Russian [[physicist]]. He is a member of the [[Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics|Landau Institute]] in [[Chernogolovka]] near [[Moscow]] in [[Russia]] and a Distinguished Professor of [[Theoretical Physics]] and holder of the William R. Thurman ’58 Chair in Physics at [[Texas A&M University]].<ref name="Gold2018">{{cite news |title=Texas A&M Physicist Valery Pokrovsky Earns 2018 Landau Gold Medal |url=https://science.tamu.edu/news/2018/03/texas-am-physicist-valery-pokrovsky-earns-2018-landau-gold-medal/ |access-date=21 March 2022 |work=Texas A&M College of Science |date=29 March 2018}}</ref> He has twice received the [[Landau Prize]] of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences|Soviet Academy of Science]], in 1984 and in 2018.

==Early life and education==
Valery Leonidovich Pokrovsky was born on 1 January 1931 to  Leonid Pokrovsky and Raisa Razumovsky in the former Soviet Union, growing up during the [[Stalinist era]] and [[World War II]]. In 1948, he became a student of the Department of Physics and Mathematics of Kharkov University. Despite a politically-motivated attempt to expel him, Pokrovsky completed his [[master's degree]], graduating from [[Kharkov University]], [[Ukrainian SSR]], [[USSR]] in May 1953.<ref name="Pokrovsky"/>

Pokrovsky and his wife, Svetlana Krylova, were then sent to [[Novosibirsk]], where Pokrovsky became a student of an exiled scientist, [[Yuri Borisovich Rumer]]. For his Ph.D. work, Pokrovsky developed a type of polynomial and extended [[Charles L. Dolph]]'s theory of optimal linear arrays.  Valery Pokrovsky defended his PhD thesis at [[Tomsk University]] in 1957.<ref name="Pokrovsky">{{cite journal |last1=Pokrovsky |first1=Valery L. |title=My Life and Science |journal=Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics |date=10 March 2022 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=15–31 |doi=10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031720-030528 |bibcode=2022ARCMP..13...15P |s2cid=247391078 |issn=1947-5454|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Career==
In 1955, Yuri Rumer's rights of citizenship were restored and he began to build up his research group. In 1957, the [[Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences|Siberian Branch of the Academy of Sciences]] of the [[USSR]] was established. Rumer became Director of its Institute of Radiophysics and Pokrovsky became an academy scientist, where he remained until 1966.<ref name="Pokrovsky"/>

In 1966, Pokrovsky was invited to join the newly founded [[Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in Chernogolovka.  He also worked with researchers at [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]].   In 1990, he spent a six-month sabbatical with [[Heiner Müller-Krumbhaar]] at the Condensed Matter Division of the Institute of Nuclear Physics in [[Jülich]], [[Germany]].  In 1992, Pokrovsky became a professor of physics at [[Texas A&M University]] in the United States, while remaining a Senior Scientist at the Landau Institute.<ref name="Pokrovsky"/>

==Research==
His areas of research are [[quantum mechanics]], [[statistical physics]], and [[condensed matter]] theory. He is best known for his pioneering and fundamental contributions to the modern theory of [[phase transition]]s, together with [[Alexander Patashinski]], in 1965, as well as the analysis of transformations between [[commensurability (mathematics)|commensurate and incommensurate]] superstructures in [[two-dimensional]] systems, the ''Pokrovsky-Talapov transition''.

==Awards==
Valery Pokrovsky received several awards, including twice receiving the [[Landau Prize]] of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences|Soviet Academy of Science]]:first in 1984 with [[Alexander Patashinski]] for work on [[phase transition]] theory and second in 2018 “for fundamental contribution to statistical physics and quantum mechanics.”<ref name="Gold2018"/> He became a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1999, and received the [[Humboldt Prize]] in 2000.<ref name="Gold2018"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Humboldt Prize |url=http://www.scientificlib.com/en/Physics/Info/HumboldtPrize.html |website=www.scientificlib.com |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Lars Onsager Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2005 "For fundamental and original contributions to statistical physics, including development of the scaling theory for correlation functions near critical points and of theories for commensurate-incommensurate phase transitions."<ref name="APS">{{cite web |title=Prize Recipient |url=https://aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Pokrovsky&first_nm=Valery&year=2005 |website=American Physical Society |access-date=21 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref>
